name: Listener crossword No 1: A Musical Crossword

clue.text: Spanish for aubade

blocks.note: the word wanted is the Spanish-language term, not the French one
an aubade is a morning song, typically sung at dawn beneath a window

explanation.walkthrough: This 1930 musical puzzle is a general-knowledge crossword, so the clue is a straight definition; the Spanish dawn serenade takes its name from alba, dawn.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain's dawn serenade, often played on pipe and drum, is the counterpart of the French morning song.

clue.text: Musicians who possess this will draw the crowds

definitions.text: Musicians who possess this will draw the crowds

blocks.note: surface reading: some skill or possession a performer might own
setter's reading: the indefinable star quality, sex appeal, that pulls in audiences

explanation.surface: Performers with a certain something sell out concert halls.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1920s the two-letter pronoun was slang for charisma or sex appeal, made famous by Clara Bow, the 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang of the period used the pronoun for magnetic personal charm, the quality that makes audiences flock to a performer.

clue.text: The parent of the Sonata

blocks.note: surface reading: a mother or father
setter's reading: the older form from which the multi-movement sonata developed

explanation.walkthrough: Music histories of the time traced the sonata back to the Baroque sequence of dance movements, so the older form is its 'parent'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Baroque set of contrasted dance movements is the historical ancestor of the sonata's movement plan.

clue.text: This music often figures in the broadcast programmes

definitions.text: This music often figures in the broadcast programmes

blocks.note: a kind of music, unnamed

blocks.clueFragment: often figures in the broadcast programmes
blocks.note: BBC wireless schedules in 1930 regularly carried late-evening band music for listeners to move to

explanation.surface: A style of music turns up again and again in the wireless listings.
explanation.walkthrough: Puzzle printed in the BBC's own magazine; its nightly dance-band broadcasts were a fixture, and 'figures' quietly hints at the steps of a ballroom routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballroom band music, played for foxtrots and waltzes, filled much of the evening airtime on 1930 radio.

clue.text: An opera by a Russian composer

definitions.text: An opera by a Russian composer

blocks.note: a stage work, title wanted
Rimsky-Korsakov, whose fairy-tale opera of 1900 is usually titled The Tale of Tsar Saltan

explanation.surface: A general request for any Russian opera.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual English title spells the ruler's name Saltan; this grid uses the variant spelling with U. The flight of the bumblebee comes from this opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Rimsky-Korsakov's 1900 fairy-tale stage work is named after its royal hero, from a Pushkin poem.

clue.text: An English composer of anthems

blocks.note: a name wanted, from English church music
an early eighteenth-century Gloucester Cathedral organist who wrote church anthems

explanation.surface: A straightforward question about English church music.
explanation.walkthrough: An anthem here means a choral piece for the Anglican service, not a national song.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hine, early eighteenth-century Gloucester Cathedral organist, is remembered for his choral church pieces.

clue.text: Quickly

blocks.note: everyday reading: at speed
musical reading: the Italian tempo marking for a fast pace

explanation.walkthrough: In a musical puzzle the English adverb points to its Italian tempo-marking equivalent, the kind of word printed above a score.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian tempo direction instructs performers to play very fast, faster than allegro.

clue.text: A semibreve in Common Time

blocks.note: a whole note, worth four crotchet beats
common time is 4/4, so a whole note fills an entire measure and can occur only one time per measure

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a request for a definition of the note; the answer is instead how often it can appear. A bar is the British term for a measure.
explanation.definitionFit: In four-four time the whole note lasts the full measure, so its frequency is a single occurrence per measure.

clue.text: Singers sometimes have to do this

definitions.text: Singers sometimes have to do this

blocks.clueFragment: Singers sometimes have to do this
blocks.note: surface reading: some musical task, like transposing or holding a note
setter's reading: the throat-soothing rinse a vocalist uses before performing

explanation.surface: A remark about one of the duties of vocalists.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a question about technique; it is about throat care, where bubbling liquid makes a sound of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Vocalists rinse their throats with liquid held at the back of the mouth to ease hoarseness.

clue.text: The initials of a well-known English Musical Society

definitions.text: The initials of a well-known English Musical Society

blocks.note: only the first letters of the name are wanted

blocks.clueFragment: of a well-known English Musical Society
blocks.note: the Royal Choral Society, the big London choir based at the Royal Albert Hall

explanation.surface: A quiz about musical societies' abbreviations.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Choral Society, founded in 1871, gave the annual Messiah and Hiawatha performances at the Royal Albert Hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal Choral Society abbreviates to three letters, the famous London choir at the Albert Hall.

clue.text: Often with variations

blocks.note: frequently, so not always
a theme and variations takes a simple tune and elaborates it repeatedly

explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes the thing rather than naming it: a simple melody is the usual basis of a set of variations, as in Handel's Harmonious Blacksmith.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple tune or melody is the commonest starting point for a theme-and-variations movement.

clue.text: An opera by Sir Frederic Cowan

definitions.text: An opera by Sir Frederic Cowan

blocks.note: a stage work, title wanted
Sir Frederic Cowen (usually so spelt), English composer and conductor, wrote an opera of 1895 on the Norman Conquest

explanation.surface: A general-knowledge question about a British composer's operas.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue misspells Cowen. His opera Harold, or the Norman Conquest was staged at Covent Garden in 1895.
explanation.definitionFit: Cowen's 1895 opera is named for the English king killed at Hastings in 1066.

clue.text: Agitatedly

blocks.note: everyday reading: in a restless, upset way
musical reading: the Italian performance direction meaning restless

explanation.walkthrough: As with the other one-word adverbs here, the English points to an Italian expression mark found on a score.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian expression mark asks the performer to play in a restless, uneasy manner.

clue.text: Half of a famous opera

definitions.note: the clue gives the wordplay only; there is no separate definition in this general-knowledge puzzle

indicators.note: taking a half means losing the other half, so only two of four letters stay

blocks.note: Verdi's Egyptian opera of 1871

explanation.surface: A request for part of a well-known opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Verdi's AIDA has four letters; keep the first half, AI.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no definition: the entry is merely the first two letters of the famous Verdi title, a filler for the grid.

clue.text: Two parts on one stave

blocks.note: two instrumental lines, such as first and second flute
when both share a single staff, the Italian marking tells them to play in unison

explanation.walkthrough: A stave is the British term for a staff. The Italian marking literally means 'for two' and tells both players to take the same notes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian score marking, literally 'for two', directs two instruments sharing a staff to play together.

clue.text: An orchestra would be at sea without these

definitions.text: An orchestra would be at sea without these

blocks.clueFragment: An orchestra would be at sea
blocks.note: surface reading: lost, confused, perhaps without a conductor
setter's reading: the music stands shared by pairs of players, which hold their parts

explanation.surface: An orchestra would be all at sea without some essential thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Orchestral string players sit in pairs at a stand called a desk; without stands there is no music to read.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchestral music stands, each shared by two players, are called desks in British usage.

clue.text: For nine voices or instruments

definitions.note: the clue reads as an adjectival phrase while the answer is the noun for such a piece

blocks.note: the number of performers
the Italian term for a piece for that ensemble

explanation.walkthrough: The Italian form is wanted here, from nono, ninth; the English equivalent is shorter.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian musical term for a composition scored for an ensemble of nine performers.

clue.text: Initials of a musical society

blocks.note: only the first letters of the name are wanted
the setter does not say which

explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives no way to pin the society down, so the crossing letters decide; a likely candidate is the Edinburgh Musical Society, famous in the eighteenth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Three initial letters standing for a society devoted to music, probably the Edinburgh Musical Society.

clue.text: The title of a ballad published before the war

definitions.text: The title of a ballad published before the war

blocks.note: a song name wanted
a popular parlour ballad by Henry Trotère, from before the First World War

explanation.surface: A question about an old song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The war' means the First World War, recent memory in 1930. The title is an Irish endearment meaning 'treasure' or 'darling'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trotère's Edwardian parlour song took its title from an Irish term of endearment for a loved one.

clue.text: Caressingly

blocks.note: everyday reading: with a gentle touch
musical reading: the Italian expression mark meaning coaxing or flattering

explanation.walkthrough: As with the other one-word adverbs, an Italian expression mark is wanted; it comes from lusingare, to flatter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian expression mark asks for a coaxing, flattering, tender style of playing.

clue.text: An opera by Balfe

blocks.note: a stage work, title wanted
Michael William Balfe, the Irish composer of The Bohemian Girl

explanation.walkthrough: Balfe's lesser-known 1860 opera was Bianca, or the Bravo's Bride.
explanation.definitionFit: Balfe's 1860 romantic opera takes its title from its heroine's name.

clue.text: Anagram of old English word for a barrel organ

definitions.note: defines the word before the jumble; the grid holds its letters in a different order

indicators.note: the setter states outright that the grid letters are a rearrangement of the thing clued

blocks.note: an archaic name for a medieval instrument, applied loosely to the hurdy-gurdy and other cranked instruments

explanation.surface: A frank instruction rather than a surface.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter needed four awkward letters in the grid and asked for them as a jumble of ROTE, an archaic instrument name.
explanation.definitionFit: No real definition: the grid letters are a scrambled form of an archaic name for a hand-cranked instrument.

clue.text: A living composer

blocks.note: alive when the puzzle appeared in 1930
an Italian, composer of The Pines of Rome, who died in 1936

explanation.walkthrough: The clue alone could fit hundreds of names; in 1930 the crossings had to settle it. Ottorino Respighi wrote the Roman trilogy of tone poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Ottorino Respighi was an Italian writer of orchestral music still alive and working when this appeared.

clue.text: A major

blocks.note: everyday reading: an army officer
musical reading: the key, wanted in its German form

explanation.walkthrough: 'Major' tempts towards an army rank; the answer is the German name for the key, A-Dur, run together.
explanation.definitionFit: German names keys with Dur for the bright mode, so the key of three sharps is A-Dur.

clue.text: An English composer

blocks.note: nationality of the person wanted
a London-born professor at the Royal Academy of Music (1885-1943)

explanation.walkthrough: Benjamin Dale was known for his piano sonata and viola works; the crossings pin down the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Dale was an early twentieth-century London-born writer of piano and viola music.

clue.text: Add three letters and this becomes a famous example of 12 across

definitions.text: Add three letters and this becomes a famous example of 12 across
definitions.note: the clue defines a longer word built on the entry, not the entry itself

blocks.note: a longer word contains the entry plus three more letters
the longer word is the name of a well-known ballroom or folk step, 12 across being the music for it

explanation.walkthrough: The setter never says which dance or where the extra letters go, so the entry comes from the crossings; the clue only confirms it once the dance occurs to you.
explanation.definitionFit: The four letters are what remains of a well-known dance's name with three letters removed, so the clue defines it only indirectly.

clue.text: Popular at Covent Garden

blocks.note: surface reading: well liked, perhaps of the flower and fruit market there
setter's reading: the Royal Opera House, where star male singers drew the crowds

explanation.walkthrough: Covent Garden was both London's fruit and flower market and the site of the Royal Opera House; the clue means the opera house and its star singers.
explanation.definitionFit: Star high-voiced male opera singers, such as Caruso or Gigli, were the great favourites of opera audiences.

clue.text: A non-musical term that might well sum up much of modern music

definitions.text: A non-musical term that might well sum up much of modern music

blocks.note: a word borrowed from outside music

blocks.clueFragment: might well sum up much of modern music
blocks.note: a jibe at 1920s modernism: a word for a violent breaking-up or disruption

explanation.surface: A grumble that much of today's music is a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's dig at atonal modernism; the word, from geology, means a breaking or disruption, and sounds a little like cataclysm.
explanation.definitionFit: The geological word means a violent breaking apart, which the setter suggests describes discordant modern compositions.

clue.text: The hero of one of Plato’s myths

definitions.text: The hero of one of Plato’s myths

blocks.note: the central figure of a story
the Myth of Er, which closes Plato's Republic

explanation.walkthrough: The only non-musical clue in the grid: in the Republic a soldier killed in battle returns from death to report the afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: The Republic ends with the tale of a slain soldier who revives to describe the afterlife.

clue.text: Anagram of name of well-known promoter of concerts

definitions.note: defines the name before the jumble; the grid holds its letters in a different order

indicators.note: the setter states outright that the grid letters are a rearrangement of the thing clued

blocks.note: probably the actress Lena Ashwell, famous for organising concerts for troops at the front in the First World War

explanation.surface: A frank instruction rather than a surface.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter needed four awkward letters and asked for them as a jumble of a name; Lena Ashwell is the likeliest 1930 reading, though the clue does not make it certain.
explanation.definitionFit: No real definition: the grid letters are a scrambled form of a concert organiser's first name.

clue.text: A flute player who taught at Brussels

definitions.text: A flute player who taught at Brussels

blocks.note: a flautist, name wanted
a nineteenth-century Belgian virtuoso, professor at the Brussels Conservatoire

explanation.walkthrough: Egide Aerts was a Belgian virtuoso and composer for his instrument; a name only a specialist would know, so the crossings carry it.
explanation.definitionFit: Egide Aerts was a nineteenth-century Belgian virtuoso who held a professorship at the Brussels Conservatoire.

clue.text: Conductor of a London choir

blocks.note: a choral director, name wanted
a choir director of that surname active in London around 1930

explanation.walkthrough: The clue does not name the choir, so this is a period name settled by the crossings rather than by the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs to a choral director who led one of London's choirs at the time of publication.

clue.text: Anagram of name of a baritone who first broadcast from Manchester

definitions.note: defines the name before the jumble; the grid holds its letters in a different order

indicators.note: the setter states outright that the grid letters are a rearrangement of the thing clued

blocks.clueFragment: a baritone who first broadcast from Manchester
blocks.note: a singer heard on 2ZY, the early Manchester wireless station; Q followed by U is the only sensible order

explanation.surface: A frank instruction rather than a surface.
explanation.walkthrough: Another jumbled grid filler; the letters can only sensibly spell QUIN, a singer from the early days of Manchester radio.
explanation.definitionFit: No real definition: the grid letters are a scrambled form of an early radio singer's surname.

clue.text: The Paris Conservatoire stands in this

definitions.text: The Paris Conservatoire stands in this

blocks.note: the French national music college
its address: from 1911 it occupied a building in a Paris street named after Madrid

explanation.walkthrough: The French word for street is wanted, since the building stands on the rue de Madrid; 'stands in' tempts towards a district or city.
explanation.definitionFit: French uses this word for a street, the sort of road on which the Paris music college stood.

clue.text: First word of a famous Lenten hymn

definitions.text: First word of a famous Lenten hymn

blocks.note: only the opening word is wanted
the medieval Latin hymn on the day of wrath, a penitential text

explanation.walkthrough: Dies irae, the medieval Latin hymn on the Last Judgement, is best known from the Requiem Mass; its penitential tone links it to the season of Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for 'day' opens the famous medieval penitential hymn on judgement.

clue.text: Last three letters of Christian name of a great composer

definitions.text: Last three letters of Christian name of a great composer
definitions.note: the clue gives the wordplay only; there is no separate definition in this general-knowledge puzzle

indicators.note: keeping only the final trio means dropping every earlier letter of the word

blocks.clueFragment: Christian name of a great composer
blocks.note: Johann Sebastian Bach's middle given name

explanation.surface: A puzzle-setter's request for the tail end of a famous composer's first name.
explanation.walkthrough: Johann Sebastian Bach is the likely great composer; SEBASTIAN ends in IAN. A Christian name is a given name.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no definition: the entry is merely the tail of a famous composer's given name, a grid filler.

clue.text: Initials of a paper famous for its musical criticism

definitions.text: Initials of a paper famous for its musical criticism

blocks.note: only the first letters of a newspaper's name are wanted
the Daily Telegraph, whose music critics were highly regarded

explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Telegraph is a London daily newspaper whose music criticism, under critics such as Robin Legge, was much respected.
explanation.definitionFit: The London daily's two-word title abbreviates to two letters, and it was esteemed for its concert reviews.

clue.text: A French word that is hardly ever stressed in a song

definitions.text: A French word that is hardly ever stressed in a song

blocks.note: a word wanted in French

blocks.clueFragment: hardly ever stressed in a song
blocks.note: a short conjunction meaning 'and', which a setting of French verse almost never puts on a strong beat

explanation.walkthrough: The French for 'and' is a weak little linking word, so composers setting French text avoid placing it on accented notes.
explanation.definitionFit: The French conjunction meaning 'and' is an unimportant linking word, naturally left unaccented in vocal music.
